decided_by: Settled by an LLM against the official text and source code; the authors approved these decisions on 2026-10-04.
scope_note: The 127 cells where the current ground truth says the definition differs and the engineer chose no counterpart field are reported only, as pre-registered, and were not checked cell by cell

rows.label: same
rows.basis: bytesReceived difference multiplied by 8 gives the number of bits within the window, not bits per second; it still needs to be divided by the difference of the two timestamps, and the specification text cited by the engineer also says divide by the difference in the timestamps. This is a combination of two fields, so the description column is different definition.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The description states that jitter is determined by the standard deviation of packet arrival gaps within the window, and the collector scripts/alphartc/deploy/spec_collector.py lines 120 to 123 computes exactly the population standard deviation of arrival gaps within the window. This field is RFC 3550-style interarrival jitter, that is, exponential smoothing with a 1/16 gain applied to the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is a smoothed estimate and not a standard deviation, and multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The description states that jitter is determined by the standard deviation of packet interarrival times within the window, and lines 120 to 123 of the collector scripts/alphartc/deploy/spec_collector.py compute exactly the population standard deviation of interarrival times within the window. This field is RFC 3550-style interarrival jitter, that is, an exponential smoothing with gain 1/16 of the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is both a smoothed estimate and not a standard deviation, so multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9. webrtc-internals plots the raw getStats value and does not derive anything.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: received_interval is a local variable in the example code of Appendix A.3, not in any RTCP packet or XR block; the method given by the RFC is the difference of the extended highest sequence numbers of two reports minus the difference of cumulative packets lost (§6.4.4), which is a combination of multiple fields. In the third version, two checkers agreed on this judgment.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The source code cited by the engineer already states: sp->packet_count is the highest sequence number so far, and packets is the increment of the highest sequence number within the interval, that is, the expected packet count, including lost packets; the actual received count must further subtract lost_packets.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The description states that jitter is determined by the standard deviation of packet interarrival times within the window, and lines 120 to 123 of the collector scripts/alphartc/deploy/spec_collector.py compute exactly the population standard deviation of interarrival times within the window. This field is RFC 3550-style interarrival jitter, that is, an exponential smoothing with gain 1/16 of the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is both a smoothed estimate and not a standard deviation, so multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9. The iperf3 source comment states that it is computed per RFC 1889, sp->jitter += (d - sp->jitter)/16.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: Kernel comment "sum(delta(rcv_nxt)), or how many bytes were acked"; in tcp_input.c, bytes_received accumulates as rcv_nxt advances: duplicate segments are not counted, and out-of-order bytes that arrive early are counted only after the hole is filled. In a window with loss or reordering, it differs from the bytes received in the window by a time-varying amount that cannot be removed by multiplying by a constant. The third version judges on this basis that the definition is different.

rows.label: kind
rows.basis: The description states that feature 11 selects none when there is only a cumulative packet loss count or packet loss rate, and selects different definition only when there are burst or event-type fields. tcpi_lost is the number of segments marked lost in the send direction (tp->lost_out), and tcpi_probes is the number of zero-window probes; neither is a packet loss event or burst record.

rows.basis: twcc-stats is updated only at the sender when parsing received TWCC feedback (gstrtpsession.c calls rtp_session_process_twcc only upon receiving RTPFB TWCC), and is not produced at the receiver; the note lists values measured at the sender or reported by the peer as different definition.

This field is RFC 3550-style interarrival jitter, that is, an exponential smoothing with gain 1/16 of the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is both a smoothed estimate and not a standard deviation, so multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9. The avg-jitter source is avg = (diff + 15*avg) >> 4.

rows.label: kind
rows.basis: SDK 4.24.8 source code: RecvBitrate is the sum of receiveBitrate for audio and video of each remote user, receiveBitrate = 8 x max(0, this receiveBytes - last receiveBytes), updated every 1000 milliseconds, that is, the receive rate over the most recent second measured at this end. Feature 0 counts all inbound packets, including audio (collector v6 adds back exactly this audio that the testbed underreported), and the audio plus video total is exactly the scope of feature 0. That sentence in the description says that fields covering only a single stream also count as the same, and does not exclude aggregate fields.

rows.label: kind
rows.basis: The description allows a cumulative counter to be differenced between two adjacent readings, and the number of packets in the window does not need to be divided by time again. SDK 4.24.8 source: receivePackets directly takes the packets from the browser inbound-rtp statistics, measured locally.

rows.label: kind
rows.basis: SDK 4.24.8 source code: RecvBytes is the sum of receiveBytes for audio and video of each remote user, measured at this end; the total covers all inbound bytes, consistent with the scope of feature 2.

rows.label: same
rows.category: Given by the sender or the server
rows.basis: The current reason is that the document does not state the value range and the coefficient cannot be determined; after checking the source code the reason is stronger. SDK 4.24.8 source code: for remote video, currentPacketLossRate = B_evlr4/100, and B_evlr4 comes from the TRAFFIC_STATS response packet that the client requests from the Agora gateway via signaling every 3 seconds (the peer_delay list, which also contains the end-to-end delays B_ed and B_vd in the same entry); it is not measured by the browser on the received stream. The SDK's built-in network test multiplies this value by 100 and uses it as a percentage, which shows that the field itself is a ratio from 0 to 1. So it is a value given by the server, and by the description the definition is different; even if it were counted as the same, the coefficient would be 1, and the engineer's 0.01 is wrong.

rows.label: none

rows.label: same

This field is RFC 3550-style interarrival jitter, that is, an exponential smoothing with gain 1/16 of the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is both a smoothed estimate and not a standard deviation, so multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9. The SDK source getstats.js multiplies the browser-reported jitter by 1000 and rounds it.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: Three rate fields on the page: audioRecvBitsPerSecond, recvBitsPerSecond ("Total incoming bits per second (audio + video)"), videoRecvBitsPerSecond (video payload only). Feature 0 includes audio; when the full field is available, the full field is the answer; the video-only field systematically omits the audio portion, and the deployment audit of this project found the same thing (the twelfth definition difference, about 41 kbit/s on the testbed). The quantity measured by the engineer's field is similar, but it is not the closest one.

The original text of bytes_lastsec is "Bytes sent or received in the last second"; multiplied by 8 it is bit/s over a one-second window, the same type as precedent chrome_webrtc_internals feature 0.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The engineer filled in bytes_lastsec, which is a byte count, not a packet count. The current answer packets is the cumulative received packet count per inbound media stream; the difference is the packet count within the window.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The bytes difference gives exactly the byte count within the collection window; bytes_lastsec is the byte count of a fixed one-second window, and by "different window lengths are acceptable" it also makes sense. When both exist, the difference field that exactly matches the collection window is the answer; the engineer's field is acceptable but not closer.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The server source code computes bytes×8÷elapsed; elapsed is the entire statistical period from start_time to end_time, so it is an average over the entire period, not the rate within the window; it is not a cumulative counter, and differencing also cannot yield a within-window value.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The server only accumulates bytes on non-duplicate, non-padding-only packets; duplicate and padding bytes are recorded separately in bytes_duplicate and bytes_padding; all bytes received within the window must be the sum of the three, which is a multi-field combination. The engineer's basis cited only the proto declaration and did not look at the algorithm.

rows.label: same
rows.basis: The description states that jitter is determined by the standard deviation of intra-window packet arrival intervals, and the collector scripts/alphartc/deploy/spec_collector.py lines 120 to 123 compute exactly the population standard deviation of intra-window arrival intervals. This field is RFC 3550 style interarrival jitter, that is, exponential smoothing with a 1/16 gain applied to the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is a smoothed estimate, not a standard deviation, and multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9. The server performs 1/16 smoothing per RFC 3550 and then converts to microseconds, so the engineer's coefficient of 1 is also wrong.

rows.label: same

rows.label: kind
rows.basis: The definition of feature 5 is the minimum one-way delay so far, containing the same unknown constant offset as feature 4. The unknown constant can be zero; in simulation the sender and receiver share a clock, so the offset is exactly zero, and the quantity is still the minimum one-way delay so far. The collector itself also artificially sets the delay origin to 200 milliseconds for the first packet (spec_collector.py line 113), and the estimator only uses differences. The offset is permitted by the feature, not required by the feature.

This field is RFC 3550-style interarrival jitter, that is, an exponential smoothing with gain 1/16 of the absolute value of the transmission time difference between adjacent packets; it is both a smoothed estimate and not a standard deviation, so multiplying by a constant cannot convert it into feature 9.
